pages.title: A City and an Age
pages.content:
One of the most important developments of the Middle Ages (The Middle Ages span from the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 CE to the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by the Ottoman Turks) was the rise of Islam. Islam was born in the city of Mecca in the 7th century.

Two superpowers of the time were the Christian Romano-Byzantine Empire (395 CE–1453 CE) with its capital city Constantinople (which we now call Istanbul) and the Persians ruled by the Zoroastrian Sassanids (223 CE–651 CE). At that time, the Arabs were neighbors on the southeastern boundaries of the Byzantine Empire. They were also the neighbors of the Sassanids in the east.

The rivalry between these two superpowers exhausted both sides. On the other hand, because the Arabs lived in tribes, there was no political unity on the Arabian Peninsula.

After describing the broad background of the time, take a closer look at the city and the era in which Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) lived and Islam rose.

The city we are talking about is Mecca, and the time period is called the Age of Ignorance.

The Age of Ignorance is the pre-Islamic era in the Arabian Peninsula that covers the period from the 5th century to the beginning of the revelation in 610.

pages.title: Jahiliyyah and Mecca
pages.content:
The term is used to describe the beliefs and behaviors of the Arabs before the Islamic era. The meaning of “ignorance” is not the lack of science or the lack of knowledge. This period is called the Age of Ignorance because people did not truly know Allah and lacked justice, order, and peace in both their personal and social lives. They always sided with the powerful and the upper class. The oppressed, the weak and the poor were living a life of misery.

The Qur’an points to the ignorance and barbarism of the pre-Islamic era, as well as the violence, hatred, bloodshed, and other moral decline that dominated the lives of the pagan community.

The Jahiliyyah is the “age of barbarism.” In fact, the Prophet described Islam as the opposite of barbarism. An ignorant person is wild, is a slave to their desires, follows their animalistic feelings, and is brutal and aggressive; in other words, a “barbarian.” The opposite of this is a civilized person. Although the word “jahiliyyah” essentially describes the pre-Islamic period of the Arabs, the Prophet (pbuh) did not view it as a period of the past. On the contrary, he believed it could arise again at any moment and warned people against it.

To understand Jahiliyyah, it is necessary to describe Mecca. Mecca is in the western part of the Arabian Peninsula. This piece of land is called a peninsula because water surrounds it on three sides: the south, west, and east. (The Arabian/Persian Gulf is in the east, the Indian Ocean is in the south, and the Red Sea is in the west.)

pages.title: The Holy City
pages.content:
Mecca is the holy city of Islam. Allah chose this city to be the location of His House, the Holy Ka’ba. (See Al Imran, 96.) It was also in this city that the last Prophet, Muhammad (pbuh), was born and spent 52 years of his life; 40 years of his life in this city before his prophethood and almost 13 years after it. And here he began to spread the message of Islam.

The Qiblah, the direction Muslims face while performing their daily prayers (salah), is also in this city.

Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) loved this city so much that while leaving Mecca during his migration to Medina, he (pbuh) said: “I love you more than any other city. Had my people not forced me to leave, I would never have left you.” (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3925).

Mecca is described in the Holy Qur’an as “a valley where no crops grow” (Surah Ibrahim: 37). The Ka’ba is the main factor in the establishment of Mecca as a settlement. It can be said that city life began here only with the building of the Ka’ba.

When Prophet Abraham (pbuh) brought his son Ishmael and his wife Hagar to the city and left them there, the Zamzam water had not yet been discovered, so there was no population living there. This date is approximately in the 20th century BC.

pages.title: The Ka’ba and the Quraysh
pages.content:
After the discovery of the Zamzam water, the Jurhumites from Yemen settled in Mecca. Ishmael, who was the first offspring of Abraham (pbuh) to speak Arabic, learned the language from the Jurhumites. Later, when Ishmael grew up, Abraham (pbuh) came to the city to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba with his son. For the Arabs who accepted the religion taught by Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh), the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site; this helped the city grow rapidly. After Abraham (pbuh) invited people for pilgrimage (hajj) and completed his mission, he returned to Palestine.

Then a new tribe, the Khuza’a, came to Mecca, defeated the Jurhumites, and established their rule over the city. During the rule of this tribe, people forgot the religion of Abraham (pbuh) (monotheism) and spread idolatry throughout the city. In the 5th century, the administration of Mecca and the Ka’ba passed to the Quraysh tribe. Pre-Islamic Mecca was administered by a council of mostly wealthy merchants.

Since the surroundings of the city were not suitable for agriculture, people tried to make a living through trade.

In the period when Islam came, the Byzantine and Sassanid empires, which were the two most powerful states in the region, traded with Arabia in both the northern and southern regions.
India also played a very important role in Arabia’s trade. There were many products made in India, Indonesia, and China.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Since” Mean Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. Then choose the meaning of “Since”.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Since the surroundings of the city were not suitable for agriculture, people tried to make a living through trade.” What does “Since” mean in this sentence?
options: From the time when: It gives the starting point of trade.
Although: It introduces a surprising contrast.
Because: It gives the background reason for turning to trade.
After: It gives the next step in a sequence.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Since” can mean “because” or “from the time when”. Here it gives a reason that the reader can easily accept (the land was not suitable for farming), and the main clause gives the result (people turned to trade). The time meaning of “since” usually goes with a perfect tense: “People have traded here since the 5th century.”

feedback.correct: Correct. “Since” gives the known background reason for the economic change.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what the land and the trade have to do with each other. Is the first clause a starting time, or a reason?

languageFocusExercises.title: Marking a Long History

languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank] the discovery of the Zamzam water, the Jurhumites from Yemen settled in Mecca. … [blank], when Ishmael grew up, Abraham (pbuh) came to the city to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba with his son. … [blank] the rule of this tribe, people forgot the religion of Abraham (pbuh) (monotheism) and spread idolatry throughout the city. languageFocusExercises.explanation: “After + noun” places one event later than another (the settlement came after Zamzam was found). “Later” is an adverb that moves the story forward on its own. “During + noun” covers the whole length of a period (the rule of the Khuza’a). “In the 5th century” names a point on the timeline. “While” needs a clause, not a noun, and “since” as a time word needs a perfect tense, so neither fits these past simple sentences.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the time expressions that turn a long history into a clear account.
feedback.incorrect: Check the first two paragraphs of Chapter 4. Which blanks are followed by a noun, which one by a comma, and which one names a century?

pages.title: Mecca as a Trade Center
pages.content:
Tribes from Yemen brought these products to the coast of Yemen and they organized caravans to transport them to Iraq, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt.

Mecca began to develop into a trade center from the early 6th century CE (Common Era). Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, the great-grandfather of Muhammad (pbuh), played a key role in boosting the economy of Mecca. He, along with the leaders of the Quraysh tribe, made trade deals with some tribes and nations, and they were given permission to travel freely. These agreements also allowed Quraysh merchants to enter Byzantium, Yemen, Iraq, and Abyssinia (Ethiopia). The summer and winter journeys described in the Holy Qur’an were organized once a year with large caravans (see Surah Quraysh: 1-4). These caravans numbered up to 2,500 camels.

This meant approximately 2–3 shiploads of cargo. At that time, the typical Roman trade ship had a carrying capacity of around 100–150 tons. This number shows us how large the trade was.

In addition to these, many caravans left Mecca at almost every time of the year. For example, one of the places where the Quraysh caravans traveled for trade was Egypt, the Byzantine Empire’s wealthiest region. Abyssinia was also a place with which the Quraysh had trade relations by sea. Suhayl b. Amr and Uthman Ibn Affan were shipowners from the Quraysh tribe. So, beginning with the settlement of the Quraysh tribe in Mecca in the mid-5th century CE, the city of Mecca gradually developed into a center of trade.

pages.title: Sacred Months and Trade
pages.content:
During this period, the Silk Road—the most important of the eastern trade routes that connected the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean—became unusable in the 6th century CE due to the wars between the Byzantine and Sassanid empires. This made the Red Sea route and the overland route through Arabia highly important.

The safe environment created by the sacred months made it possible for more people to perform the Hajj. The sacred months are the four lunar months in which fighting is prohibited: Dhu al-Qadah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. During this period, people focus on worship, show respect, and refrain from sinning, so that there is an atmosphere of peace. (During the pre-Islamic Jahiliyyah period, the Arabs continued to visit the Ka’ba and the sacred sites in its neighborhood. Pagan people would walk around the Ka’ba, perform the sa’y between Safa and Marwah, and stand in Arafat.)

Hajj also meant livelier trade. In addition, major trade festivals such as Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhul-Majaz were also held during the sacred months. They were particularly held during the Hajj season, and after people attended these fairs, they went to Arafat.

Because of its extensive trade activities, Mecca was described as the “Republic of Traders.”

So, at the beginning of the 7th century, the Quraysh gained control of the most important trade route and wealth in Arabia.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “This” at the start of a sentence often sums up the whole situation in the previous sentence, so the writer can turn it into the cause of something new: The Silk Road became unusable → this made the other routes important. Using “This made …” links two causal steps into a chain instead of listing two separate facts.

pages.title: Social Classes in Mecca
pages.content:
The Quraysh used coins, as well as gold and silver, in their trade. Paying a fee to borrow money—which is usury—played a very significant role in the economic activities of the time. This practice also affected the social structure. Usury, which means additional money on the original amount of money, is “riba” in Arabic. The Quraysh added to their wealth through lending at usury. It was the easiest and most profitable way to increase one’s wealth. As a result of the money trade, there was a wealthy aristocracy in the city. In such an environment where trade and money were so important, all human relationships were based on making more money. Money lenders and capitalists were the city’s most powerful class. They imposed enormous borrowing rates on debts. This system was designed to make the rich richer and the poor poorer. Vices of drinking and gambling were also so common that this was also one reason why people were constantly falling into debt.

Because large amounts of wealth were concentrated in the hands of certain individuals, there were extreme divisions between social classes. In fact, there were rich people who ate from gold plates and drank from silver cups and crystal glasses, but there were also poor people who could barely survive.

There was a huge gap between the rich and the poor even in the most basic human relationships. Among the upper class of the Quraysh, money, wealth, children, and family were a source of pride and competition.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the sentences from Chapter 7. Does each one describe an economic practice, or the social result of such practices?

Economic practice: The Quraysh added to their wealth through lending at usury.

Social result: This system was designed to make the rich richer and the poor poorer.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter first describes practices (lending at usury, imposing enormous borrowing rates) and then their effects on the whole society (a huge gap, extreme contrasts between luxury and survival). “This system was designed to make the rich richer and the poor poorer” is a result stated as a purpose: The two comparatives moving in opposite directions show a gap that widens both ways, and “was designed to” is the writer’s strong interpretation that the result was not an accident.

pages.title: Injustice and Hilf al-Fudul
pages.content:
Even when Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) began calling people to Islam, these people said, “With men like us around, is it really up to Muhammad to become the leader of the Quraysh?” (see Surah Zukhruf: 31)

In such a society, orphans were oppressed, the weak were looked down on, and the poor were shown no mercy. For instance, the camels of the weak used to be taken without payment, and the goods and property of small sellers were unjustly seized by force. Furthermore, the weak and defenseless people who came to the city from outside for pilgrimage and trade were unfairly treated and oppressed. To prevent such incidents, an agreement was made by some Quraysh tribes to help people who had been oppressed in Mecca. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), who was twenty years old at the time, also attended this meeting. This formation was named Hilf al-Fudul, which means The Community of the Righteous. Young Muhammad became an enthusiastic member of the organization.

During the pre-Islamic era, those who oppressed and treated people unfairly were generally wealthy and powerful individuals. Due to its fight against injustice, Hilf al-Fudul received support from the community.

This organization played a very important role in maintaining justice and order in Mecca and tried to protect the rights of the oppressed. For example, a merchant had sold goods to Ubayy b. Khalaf, one of Mecca’s leading figures, but had not received payment. The merchant, having no other option, turned to Hilf al-Fudul for help. The members of the organization told him to go to Ubayy and demand his money again, and to inform him that if he did not pay, they would collect it themselves.

pages.title: Generosity and Tribal Life
pages.content:
On this, Ubayy paid the money immediately. This formation also made Mecca a safer city for trade.

All sources note that the Prophet (pbuh) spoke highly of this formation even after his prophethood and believed that Islam had further strengthened it. He used to say: “I have no desire to abandon my oath even against a herd of red-haired camels.” It is recorded that he said he would respond immediately without hesitation if he were called again (Musnad, I, 190, 317).

As the example of the Hilf al-Fudul shows, it certainly doesn’t make sense to call the pre-Islamic era entirely negative. In addition to this, for instance, the Arabs before Islam were known for their extraordinary generosity and hospitality. They used to bet on who could slay and offer the most camels for their guests. The bet was a type of gambling as well. Until one side gave up, camels continued to be slaughtered, and at the end, the victor became well-known for his generosity. All of this was done for the fame of the individual and the tribe.

The admirable qualities of the Arabs before Islam, like generosity, were driven mostly by arrogance rather than real goodness. In the end, such behaviors turned into a tribal honor contest, and this led to greater problems.

Tribes were the basis of Arab society.

pages.title: Women in Jahiliyyah
pages.content:
In the hard desert environment, physical strength was crucial. So men were seen as the tribes' most valuable fighting members. The Arabs' main aim was to have a large number of male children because this was the only way they could be respected by other tribes. Without tribal protection, people could not protect their lives and property.

Pre-Islamic Arabs valued ancestors greatly and knew their names by heart. It was important to work for the tribe and to honor and defend it in every circumstance, no matter what the tribe did.

The position of Arab women before Islam was not always the same. It changed according to their social status and tribes. Despite limitations from society, some women managed to gain a degree of freedom. For example, Khadija, the wealthy wife of the Prophet (pbuh), was free to run a business under her own name. Or a woman from a higher social class, like Hind bint Utbah, who was the wife of Abu Sufyan and the mother of Mu’awiya, had some power in society.

However, many women from lower social and economic groups were mistreated and disadvantaged. Those women and girls had no status and no human or legal rights in their family lives and in society. They had no say and were not allowed to give their opinions.

When news of the birth of a daughter was given to them, people in the Age of Ignorance lamented and their faces were darkened with grief and fury. They themselves were ashamed of having daughters and longed for sons to increase their power and dignity.

pages.title: Slavery, Poets and Media
pages.content:
The Holy Qur’an describes this scene in Surah Nahl, verses 58-59: “And when one of them is given news of a female baby, his face darkens, and he can’t breathe with grief. He hides from the people because of the bad news given to him. Shall he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Evil is the decision they make.”

Slavery was an economic institution in Mecca. Slaves, both male and female, were the most miserable class in society. They were bought and sold like animals. They were employed in various tasks as well as for people’s personal service. They were a show of wealth. They also acted as weapons to protect their owners in times of war. White slaves brought from the regions of Damascus and Iraq were more expensive than black slaves brought from Africa because they served better and were skilled workers.

During this era, poets were an important part of social life and poetry was the most important part of the culture. Poetry was used to keep the tribe’s history alive. It told stories about brave ancestors and hard times. It also praised the tribe’s family and criticized enemies. Tribes were honored in poems, and poets praised conflict and war rather than peace. There were very few poets who invited the tribes to peace and urged them to stay away from fighting. In a sense, they were serving as a media outlet. Tribes often formed a political alliance to defend each other, yet extreme tribalism made universal justice impossible when people supported their tribe even when it was wrong.

pages.title: Religious Life in Mecca
pages.content:
Arabia was idolatrous; only a few individuals had adopted religions like Christianity. In Mecca there were some Hanifs who believed in the religion of Abraham (pbuh), but idolatry was dominant. The number of idols in and around the Ka’ba reached 360, including Lat, Manat, and Uzza. These idols were respected by all tribes. There were idols in many houses too.

Actually, the Arabs of the Age of Ignorance accepted the presence of a higher God known as “Allah.” Although they mainly worshipped idols, they believed “Allah” to be the creator. Idols were seen as go-betweens (mediators). Oddly enough they did not believe in the Resurrection and Afterlife. Before Islam, stones were placed in front of the Ka’ba and people worshipped in groups.

No doubt, pilgrimage to the Ka’ba was the most popular and common form of worship. Every tribe walked around the Ka’ba during the pilgrimage season, when fighting was forbidden and disputes between the tribes ended. They stopped in front of their own gods, offered a prayer, and bowed respectfully. Walking around the Ka’ba was generally performed naked to symbolize purification from sins.

Superstitious beliefs also dominated Arab life. Pre-Islamic Arabs thought the gods talked through kahins (soothsayers) and poets who had godly guidance and could predict the future. Before doing anything, people sought omens.

pages.title: Islam and a New Society
pages.content:
Politics, economics, and religion are three interconnected areas. Religion and beliefs determine every aspect of life. So, it is understandable that Islam faced opposition from both politically and economically powerful groups in Mecca. From the start, Islam showed that this was a new group. Islam made this new Muslim community different from, and better than, the people around them.

The aristocracy provoked the public against the new religion. The leaders of the Quraysh viewed Islam as a threat to their authority. The wealth they got through trade, as well as the respect they received from other tribes, made the Quraysh the leaders of their region. They were serving as the prestigious caretakers of the pilgrimage in the Arabian Peninsula. Protecting this status and unity was very important to them.

The first people who heard the Prophet’s call, which began in 610, were the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. Some of the Quraysh responded positively to his call and became Muslims. When they heard the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) read the Qur’an, they were sure it was from Allah. This message totally changed them. It touched their hearts and minds, making them cry and feel deep respect, even causing their hair to stand on end. However, a large group led by the tribal leaders denied his prophethood and opposed him fiercely.

pages.title: Quraysh and Power
pages.content:
The population of Mecca, where the Prophet (pbuh) taught Islam for 13 years, was between 5,000 and 10,000. In the first few years of the call to Islam, there was almost no one from Mecca’s super-rich among the 46 people who became Muslims. Many of the first Muslims were the poor and the slaves. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) mentioned Allah’s infinite Mercy, Wisdom, Goodness and Power. This filled their hearts with joy and hope.

The upper class of the city, whose survival depended on the existing order, refused to accept the rise of a new formation and opposed it violently.

Indeed, almost none of the tribal leaders had accepted Islam. Although the leading figures of the Quraysh were not always extremely wealthy, they were prominent figures within the Quraysh, like Abu Talib.

The new belief system was introducing radical changes in every area. For instance, the Quraysh considered usury to be lawful and said, “Trade is like usury.” The Qur’an, however, distinguishes between usury and trade; it emphasizes that trade is halal (lawful) while usury is haram (unlawful). These people, who saw themselves as superior to others because of their wealth, ignored the Qur’an’s commands to be fair to the poor, to pay zakat, and to give alms as ways to purify their wealth.

Maintaining their leadership position was of vital importance to the leaders of the Quraysh. The Quraysh were saying, “Muhammad is trying to gain the upper hand over us; he wants us to obey him and become the ultimate authority over us. Never obey him.”

pages.title: Opposition to the New Faith
pages.content:
They knew that the Prophet’s call to monotheism—which rejected oppression, injustice, exploitation, and usury—would eventually bring them face to face with people who carried out these practices.

Pagan Meccan leaders tried various methods to prevent the new faith from growing stronger. At first, they mocked just the new religion. When the Prophet (pbuh) passed by the places where the disbelievers were sitting, they would point and laugh at him and say, “The son of the family of Abd al-Muttalib is bringing news from heaven!”

However, when the Qur’an began to speak ill of their idols, mock them, and announce that they and their idols would be fuel for Hell, they began to oppose him fiercely. Poor people or those without powerful protectors suffered the most. One of them was Bilal, an Abyssinian slave. He became one of the first believers in Islam. His master, Umayya b. Khalaf, often took him out in the hot midday sun. He put a heavy rock on Bilal’s chest and ordered him to give up his religion.

The Meccan elites went further and imposed a social and economic boycott on the Muslims and those who protected the Prophet (pbuh) between 617 and 620. During this period the Prophet (pbuh), his wife Khadija, and Abu Talib spent all their wealth to support the Muslims. Some people died of starvation; there were even those who ate tree leaves. The cries of children dying of hunger began to be heard.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “At first” marks the earliest, mildest stage (mockery). “However, when …” marks a turning point: Once the idols were challenged, the opposition became fierce. pages.title: Hostility and Tribal Fanaticism
pages.content:
One of the main reasons for the Quraysh’s hostility toward the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was the Qur’an’s demand that they abandon their old false religions about which they boasted at every opportunity. The other was the Qur’an’s call for them to worship a single Allah.

The rejection of idols meant, for the Quraysh, the end of the trade on which they depended for their wealth. Leaders who built their authority on idols would lose both their political and economic influence if they lost their idols.

They also refused to believe that they would face punishment in the afterlife for their sins. It was too much for them to think that they would be judged for oppressing people, gaining money through unjust means, as well as for drinking alcohol and every kind of evil.

As mentioned above, one of the characteristics of Arab society was tribal fanaticism. This was also one of the greatest barriers for the new religion. A tribal member could not show the courage to step outside the views of his tribe. Otherwise, he would be left unprotected by his tribe—which, in today’s terms, means being stateless and being left defenseless. The leaders in Mecca tried everything to stop the new Muslims. Because of this, the “freedom of choice” that Islam talked about could not work at that time.

pages.title: Islam Against Ignorance
pages.content:
For example, Abu Jahl, one of the leading figures of opposition to Islam, strongly rejected Islam and led his tribe in the same direction. The Quraysh were saying that Islam broke up families and because of this, the Quraysh lost power. When the Quraysh leaders blamed the Prophet, they said, “You have destroyed our unity.”

In Mecca, which was a place of oppression, injustice, and immorality before Islam, the Prophet (pbuh) called upon people to follow justice and morality. At the heart of Islam is human honor and dignity. Islam respects humans as humans. All other differences are not important to Islam. Whether they are slaves, women, poor, or the weak, they all deserve respect.

The Age of Ignorance was the opposite of Islam. The term both refers to pre-Islamic Arabia and also describes any culture, society or way of thinking that comes from human arrogance. On the other hand, Islam is all about making the world a fairer and more peaceful place.

The dreadful situation in the twenty-first century reminds us of the dark period of ignorance in seventh-century Mecca. So, the Age of Ignorance is not only a period in the past but also a way of thinking that can still exist today. Islam has always stood against it and will continue to do so.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Both … and also” holds the historical meaning and the wider meaning together. “Whether … or …” includes every group. “On the other hand” turns to the opposing side. “Has always … and will continue” joins past, present and future. “Reminds us of” marks a comparison between today and seventh-century Mecca: It is an analogy the writer draws, not historical evidence.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed how the conclusion extends, includes, contrasts, spans time and compares.
feedback.incorrect: Reread paragraphs 2–4 of Chapter 17. Focus on the key signals: both … and also, whether … or, on the other hand, has always … will continue, reminds us of.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting and Identifying
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the new sentence. Keep the meaning of the original.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these sentences from Chapter 17?

transformItems.source: When the Quraysh leaders blamed the Prophet, they said, “You have destroyed our unity.”
transformItems.frame: When the Quraysh leaders blamed the Prophet, they said that he [blank] their unity.

transformItems.source: For example, Abu Jahl, one of the leading figures of opposition to Islam, strongly rejected Islam and led his tribe in the same direction.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: When direct speech is reported after a past verb (they said that …), the present perfect moves back to the past perfect and the pronouns change: “You have destroyed our unity” → “he had destroyed their unity”. Reporting also reminds the reader that this is the leaders’ accusation, not the writer’s view. The phrase “one of the leading figures …” is a shortened relative clause (who was one of …) that identifies Abu Jahl.

feedback.correct: Well done. You reported the accusation and expanded the identifying phrase.
feedback.incorrect: In the first frame, move the tense one step back after “they said that”. In the second, add a relative pronoun and a verb for a person in the past.

languageFocusExercises.title: Synthesize Across Time
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say six or seven sentences about the word “Jahiliyyah”, then and now.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Jahiliyyah mean then, and what can it mean today?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: B2 synthesis should keep historical description, conceptual extension and present-day comparison distinct but connected.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the chapter language and relationship accurately.
feedback.incorrect: Not yet. Return to the chapter wording and check the relationship the form expresses.

discussionPrompts.question: Say what it meant then, then today. Use “both … and”, “whether … or” and “on the other hand”.
discussionPrompts.example: Historically, Jahiliyyah refers to pre-Islamic Arabia, from the 5th century to the beginning of the revelation in 610. At that time, Mecca was a place of oppression, injustice and immorality. The chapter, however, uses the term both for that period and also for any way of thinking that comes from human arrogance. Islam teaches that all people deserve respect, whether they are slaves, women, poor or weak. On the other hand, people in the Age of Ignorance always sided with the powerful and the upper class. As its concluding analogy, the chapter compares the dreadful situation of the twenty-first century with seventh-century Mecca. In this view, the Age of Ignorance can still exist today, and Islam will continue to stand against it.

groupTask.title: A Pact for Our School

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You reread Chapters 8–9 and copy one sentence about Hilf al-Fudul exactly as it is written.

roles.name: Pact Writer
roles.job: You write the pact: The problem, whom it protects, what members promise and what happens if a promise is not kept.

roles.name: Presenter

steps: Reread Chapters 8–9 and copy one sentence exactly, for example: “To prevent such incidents, an agreement was made by some Quraysh tribes to help people who had been oppressed in Mecca.”
Choose one real problem at school that a pact could answer, such as students who are left out or not listened to. Do not name any real classmate.

Write a one-page pact: What problem it answers, whom it protects, what members promise to do and what happens if the promise is not kept. Use patterns such as a passive without ‘by’ (Students are left out …), ‘If …, we will …’ and ‘mostly … rather than …’.
Read the pact aloud in your group and improve one sentence. Nobody speaks as a person from the story; you only quote the book and write your own pact.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its pact in two minutes, reads its quote from the book and explains which part of the pact the quote inspired.
groupTask.solo: Copy one sentence about Hilf al-Fudul from Chapters 8–9, then write a short pact for your school with a problem, a promise and a clear result if the promise is not kept.

legend.route:caravanNorth: Caravans from Yemen to Syria and Palestine

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Mecca is in the western part of the Arabian Peninsula. Allah chose it to be the location of His House, the Holy Ka’ba, and the Qur’an describes it as “a valley where no crops grow”. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was born here and spent 52 years of his life here. In the Hajj season, pagan Arabs also stood in Arafat, and major trade festivals such as Ukaz, Majannah and Dhul-Majaz were held during the sacred months.
places.teacherNote: Arafat and the fair sites are not drawn because the book does not give their locations; chapter 6 only says people attended the fairs and then went to Arafat. Chapter 3 dates Abraham (pbuh) leaving Hagar and Ishmael here to about the 20th century BC.
places.question: Why can we say that city life in Mecca began with the building of the Ka’ba?

places.name: Medina
places.text: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) loved Mecca very much. While leaving Mecca during his migration to Medina, he said: “I love you more than any other city. Had my people not forced me to leave, I would never have left you.”
places.teacherNote: B2 mentions Medina only once (chapter 3) and gives no year for the migration. The line from Mecca is only a guide.
places.question: What do these words tell us about the Prophet’s (pbuh) feelings for Mecca?

places.name: Yemen
places.text: After the discovery of Zamzam water, the Jurhumites from Yemen settled in Mecca, and Ishmael (pbuh) learned Arabic from them. Tribes from Yemen also brought products made in India, Indonesia and China to the coast of Yemen. From there, they organized caravans to Iraq, Syria, Palestine and Egypt.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say which way the Jurhumites traveled or which stops the caravans used, so all lines are only a guide. Chapter 4 says the Khuza’a later defeated the Jurhumites, but it does not say where they came from.
places.question: Why was the coast of Yemen important for trade?

places.name: Abyssinia
places.text: Abyssinia (Ethiopia) was one of the lands that trade agreements allowed Quraysh merchants to enter. The Quraysh had trade relations with Abyssinia by sea, and Suhayl b. Amr and Uthman Ibn Affan were shipowners from the Quraysh tribe.
places.teacherNote: The book names no port, so the line across the Red Sea is only a guide. In chapter 15 the book calls Bilal “an Abyssinian slave”.
places.question: Why did the Quraysh need ships for their trade with Abyssinia?

places.name: Egypt
places.text: Egypt was the Byzantine Empire’s wealthiest region. It was one of the places where Quraysh caravans traveled for trade, and caravans from Yemen carried goods there too. Many caravans left Mecca at almost every time of the year.
places.teacherNote: The soft area is approximate. Chapter 6 adds that the Silk Road, which connected the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean, became unusable in the 6th century because of the wars between the Byzantine and Sassanid empires.
places.question: Why was Egypt an attractive place for Quraysh merchants?

places.name: Iraq
places.text: Caravans from Yemen carried goods to Iraq, and trade agreements allowed Quraysh merchants to enter Iraq too. Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, the great-grandfather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), played a key role in these agreements and in boosting the economy of Mecca.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 1 also says the Arabs were neighbors of the Sassanids in the east; the Sassanid lands are not drawn. The route line is only a guide.
places.question: How did the trade agreements of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf change life in Mecca?

places.name: Constantinople
places.text: Constantinople, which we now call Istanbul, was the capital of the Christian Romano-Byzantine Empire (395–1453). The Byzantines and the Zoroastrian Sassanids were the two superpowers of the time, and their rivalry exhausted both sides. The Arabs were neighbors on the southeastern boundaries of the Byzantine Empire.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 1 also says that the Middle Ages ended with the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by the Ottoman Turks. The Sassanid Empire (223–651) is not drawn; the book only says it was the Arabs’ neighbor in the east.
places.question: Why does chapter 1 describe the two superpowers before it talks about Mecca?

challenge.prompt: Find Medina, where Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) migrated when he left Mecca.
Find Constantinople, the Byzantine capital that we now call Istanbul.
Find Egypt, the Byzantine Empire’s wealthiest region and a goal of Quraysh caravans.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your understanding of the whole book through eight questions. Read each option closely and choose the one the text supports.

exercises.title: What “Ignorance” Means
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that best reflects Chapter 2.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 2, what does “ignorance” mean in the name “Age of Ignorance”?
options: A lack of science and formal knowledge among the Arabs of the time
Not truly knowing Allah, and lacking justice, order and peace in life
The period before the Arabs began to write down their poetry
The lack of political unity caused by the rivalry of two empires
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “The meaning of “ignorance” is not the lack of science or the lack of knowledge. This period is called the Age of Ignorance because people did not truly know Allah and lacked justice, order, and peace in both their personal and social lives.”

feedback.correct: Well done. The writer explicitly rules out the everyday meaning of the word: Jahiliyyah names a spiritual and moral condition, not a gap in knowledge.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 2. The writer first says what “ignorance” does not mean, and then what it does mean.

exercises.title: Leaving Mecca
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that best reflects Chapter 3.
exercises.question: What do the Prophet’s (pbuh) words on leaving Mecca during the migration make clear about his departure?
options: He left because Medina offered him better conditions for trade.
He intended to return only once the city had changed its leaders.
He had come to love Medina more than any other city.
He would never have left if his people had not forced him to.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3 quotes him (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3925): “I love you more than any other city. Had my people not forced me to leave, I would never have left you.” The unreal conditional shows that the departure was forced on him, not chosen.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Had my people not forced me to leave …” describes the opposite of what happened: He did leave, and only because he was forced to.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the Prophet’s (pbuh) words in Chapter 3, especially the second sentence. What condition made him leave?

exercises.title: Accident or Design?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement accurately reflects the writer’s view.
exercises.question: In Chapter 7, the writer presents the widening gap between rich and poor as an unintended side effect of trade rather than the purpose of the lending system.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 is explicit: “This system was designed to make the rich richer and the poor poorer.” The verb designed presents the outcome as intended, not accidental.

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. By choosing the word “designed”, the writer presents inequality as the aim of the usury system, not as an accident.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the verb the writer uses about the usury system in the first paragraph of Chapter 7. Does it suggest accident or intention?

exercises.title: An Alliance Confirmed
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that best reflects Chapter 9.
exercises.question: According to the sources the writer cites, how did the Prophet (pbuh) view Hilf al-Fudul after his prophethood?
options: He saw it as a custom of the Jahiliyyah that Islam had made unnecessary.
He respected its aims but regretted taking part in it as a young man.
He supported it mainly because it had made Mecca safer for trade.
He praised it, believed Islam had strengthened it and would answer its call.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “All sources note that the Prophet (pbuh) spoke highly of this formation even after his prophethood and believed that Islam had further strengthened it.” It is also recorded that he would respond “immediately without hesitation if he were called again.”

feedback.correct: Well done. His continued support shows that the book treats this pre-Islamic alliance for justice as something Islam confirmed, not replaced.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 9. What did the Prophet (pbuh) say and believe about the alliance after his prophethood?

exercises.title: Valuing People
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that best connects Chapters 11 and 17.
exercises.question: Chapter 11 says slaves from Damascus and Iraq cost more than slaves from Africa. Which later idea in the book stands in direct contrast to this way of valuing people?
options: Tribes formed political alliances to defend one another.
Trade is lawful, while usury is unlawful.
Human honor and dignity do not depend on origin or status.
Wealth brought the Quraysh respect from other tribes.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 reports a market that priced people by origin: “White slaves brought from the regions of Damascus and Iraq were more expensive than black slaves brought from Africa.” Chapter 17 answers this: “At the heart of Islam is human honor and dignity. Islam respects humans as humans.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Chapter 11 shows people being priced by where they came from; Chapter 17 places human honor and dignity at the heart of Islam, whatever a person’s origin.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Ask which option is about how people should be valued. Then compare Chapter 11 with the second paragraph of Chapter 17.

exercises.title: Belief and Opposition
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that best connects Chapters 12 and 16.
exercises.question: Chapter 16 says the leaders refused to believe they would face punishment in the afterlife. Which detail about religious life in Chapter 12 is consistent with this?
options: The idols in and around the Ka’ba were respected by all tribes.
The Arabs of that time did not believe in the Resurrection.
People sought omens before doing anything important.
Some Hanifs in Mecca believed in the religion of Abraham (pbuh).
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “Oddly enough they did not believe in the Resurrection and Afterlife.” Chapter 16: “They also refused to believe that they would face punishment in the afterlife for their sins.”

feedback.correct: Well done. A society that did not believe in the Resurrection had little reason to fear judgement, which helps explain the leaders’ resistance in Chapter 16.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Every option is true of Chapter 12, but only one is about life after death. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 12.

exercises.title: The First Believers
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement accurately reflects the text.
exercises.question: Chapter 14 indicates that Islam first spread mainly among Mecca’s wealthiest families, who then brought in the poor.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 14: “In the first few years of the call to Islam, there was almost no one from Mecca’s super-rich among the 46 people who became Muslims. Many of the first Muslims were the poor and the slaves.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. The movement went the other way: The first believers were largely the poor and the enslaved, while the super-rich stayed away.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 14. Who were many of the first Muslims, and how many of the super-rich joined in the first years?

exercises.title: What the Leaders Knew
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement accurately reflects the text.
exercises.question: The opening of Chapter 15 suggests that the leaders saw the call to monotheism as a threat to practices they themselves profited from.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 15: “They knew that the Prophet’s call to monotheism—which rejected oppression, injustice, exploitation, and usury—would eventually bring them face to face with people who carried out these practices.” Chapter 7 shows who profited: “The Quraysh added to their wealth through lending at usury.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The call rejected usury and exploitation, the very practices that had made the Quraysh elite rich, so the leaders knew it would confront them.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first sentence of Chapter 15 and compare it with Chapter 7. Who carried out the practices that the call to monotheism rejected?

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place before the Vocabulary Challenge.

vocabulary.definition: The historical period between the fall of the Roman Empire and the conquest of Constantinople.
vocabulary.storyExample: One of the most important developments of the Middle Ages (The Middle Ages span from the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 CE to the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by the Ottoman Turks) was the rise of Islam.

vocabulary.definition: States with enough political, military, and economic influence to shape events far beyond their own borders.
vocabulary.storyExample: Two superpowers of the time were the Christian Romano-Byzantine Empire (395 CE–1453 CE) with its capital city Constantinople (which we now call Istanbul) and the Persians ruled by the Zoroastrian Sassanids (223 CE–651 CE).

vocabulary.definition: Sustained competition between powers seeking greater influence, advantage, or control.
vocabulary.storyExample: The rivalry between these two superpowers exhausted both sides.

vocabulary.definition: The condition in which separate groups operate under a shared political authority or governing structure.
vocabulary.storyExample: On the other hand, because the Arabs lived in tribes, there was no political unity on the Arabian Peninsula.

vocabulary.definition: Divine guidance communicated by Allah to a prophet.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Age of Ignorance is the pre-Islamic era in the Arabian Peninsula that covers the period from the 5th century to the beginning of the revelation in 610.

vocabulary.definition: The acquisition of control over a territory through military force.
vocabulary.storyExample: One of the most important developments of the Middle Ages (The Middle Ages span from the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 CE to the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by the Ottoman Turks) was the rise of Islam.

vocabulary.definition: The Age of Ignorance before Islam.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Jahiliyyah is the “age of barbarism.

vocabulary.definition: A condition characterized by severe violence, cruelty, and the breakdown of civilized restraint.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an points to the ignorance and barbarism of the pre-Islamic era, as well as the violence, hatred, bloodshed, and other moral decline that dominated the lives of the pagan community.

vocabulary.definition: Subjected to persistent unjust treatment or control by a more powerful person or group.
vocabulary.storyExample: The oppressed, the weak and the poor were living a life of misery.

vocabulary.definition: A deterioration in the ethical standards and conduct expected within a society.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an points to the ignorance and barbarism of the pre-Islamic era, as well as the violence, hatred, bloodshed, and other moral decline that dominated the lives of the pagan community.

vocabulary.definition: A piece of land surrounded by water on three sides.
vocabulary.storyExample: Mecca is in the western part of the Arabian Peninsula.

vocabulary.definition: Organized according to developed social institutions, norms, and forms of public order.
vocabulary.storyExample: The opposite of this is a civilized person.

vocabulary.definition: Sacred and connected with worship.
vocabulary.storyExample: Mecca is the holy city of Islam.

vocabulary.definition: The Holy House of Allah in Mecca.
vocabulary.storyExample: Allah chose this city to be the location of His House, the Holy Ka’ba.

vocabulary.definition: The direction Muslims face during prayer.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qiblah, the direction Muslims face while performing their daily prayers (salah), is also in this city.

vocabulary.definition: A move from one place to live in another; here, the Prophet’s (pbuh) journey from Mecca to Medina.
vocabulary.storyExample: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) loved this city so much that while leaving Mecca during his migration to Medina, he (pbuh) said: “I love you more than any other city.

vocabulary.definition: A place where people begin to live.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Ka’ba is the main factor in the establishment of Mecca as a settlement.

vocabulary.definition: A child or descendant.
vocabulary.storyExample: Ishmael, who was the first offspring of Abraham (pbuh) to speak Arabic, learned the language from the Jurhumites.

vocabulary.definition: To build or form something again after it has been damaged, lost, or altered.
vocabulary.storyExample: Later, when Ishmael grew up, Abraham (pbuh) came to the city to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba with his son.

vocabulary.definition: A journey made to a sacred place for religious purposes.
vocabulary.storyExample: For the Arabs who accepted the religion taught by Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh), the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site; this helped the city grow rapidly.

vocabulary.definition: The religious practice of worshipping idols or treating them as objects of devotion.
vocabulary.storyExample: During the rule of this tribe, people forgot the religion of Abraham (pbuh) (monotheism) and spread idolatry throughout the city.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people with the same language and ancestors.
vocabulary.storyExample: Then a new tribe, the Khuza’a, came to Mecca, defeated the Jurhumites, and established their rule over the city.

vocabulary.definition: Groups of people and animals traveling together, especially to carry goods.
vocabulary.storyExample: Tribes from Yemen brought these products to the coast of Yemen and they organized caravans to transport them to Iraq, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt.

vocabulary.definition: A place where buying and selling are very important.
vocabulary.storyExample: Mecca began to develop into a trade center from the early 6th century CE (Common Era).

vocabulary.definition: Increasing or improving something.
vocabulary.storyExample: Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, the great-grandfather of Muhammad (pbuh), played a key role in boosting the economy of Mecca.

vocabulary.definition: People who buy and sell goods.
vocabulary.storyExample: These agreements also allowed Quraysh merchants to enter Byzantium, Yemen, Iraq, and Abyssinia (Ethiopia).

vocabulary.definition: Goods carried by ship, camel, or vehicle.
vocabulary.storyExample: This meant approximately 2–3 shiploads of cargo.

vocabulary.definition: The largest amount that a ship or vehicle can carry.
vocabulary.storyExample: At that time, the typical Roman trade ship had a carrying capacity of around 100–150 tons.

vocabulary.definition: An important trade route connecting East and West.
vocabulary.storyExample: During this period, the Silk Road—the most important of the eastern trade routes that connected the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean—became unusable in the 6th century CE due to the wars between the Byzantine and Sassanid empires.

vocabulary.definition: Four lunar months during which fighting was prohibited.
vocabulary.storyExample: The sacred months are the four lunar months in which fighting is prohibited: Dhu al-Qadah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab.

vocabulary.definition: Not allowed.
vocabulary.storyExample: The sacred months are the four lunar months in which fighting is prohibited: Dhu al-Qadah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab.

vocabulary.definition: Large gatherings where people buy and sell goods.
vocabulary.storyExample: In addition, major trade festivals such as Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhul-Majaz were also held during the sacred months.

vocabulary.definition: Large in scale, range, or degree.
vocabulary.storyExample: Because of its extensive trade activities, Mecca was described as the “Republic of Traders.

vocabulary.definition: A trade or travel route across land rather than sea.
vocabulary.storyExample: This made the Red Sea route and the overland route through Arabia highly important.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of lending money on exploitative or religiously prohibited interest terms.
vocabulary.storyExample: Paying a fee to borrow money—which is usury—played a very significant role in the economic activities of the time.

vocabulary.definition: Gathered in one place or in the hands of a few people.
vocabulary.storyExample: Because large amounts of wealth were concentrated in the hands of certain individuals, there were extreme divisions between social classes.

vocabulary.definition: A socially dominant upper class whose status is based on wealth, lineage, or inherited influence.
vocabulary.storyExample: As a result of the money trade, there was a wealthy aristocracy in the city.

vocabulary.definition: People who own or control capital and use it to generate profit.
vocabulary.storyExample: Money lenders and capitalists were the city’s most powerful class.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people with a similar economic or social position.
vocabulary.storyExample: Because large amounts of wealth were concentrated in the hands of certain individuals, there were extreme divisions between social classes.

vocabulary.definition: Forced something on others by authority or power.
vocabulary.storyExample: They imposed enormous borrowing rates on debts.

vocabulary.definition: Children whose parents have died.
vocabulary.storyExample: In such a society, orphans were oppressed, the weak were looked down on, and the poor were shown no mercy.

vocabulary.definition: Lacking sufficient means, power, or protection to resist harm or exploitation.
vocabulary.storyExample: Furthermore, the weak and defenseless people who came to the city from outside for pilgrimage and trade were unfairly treated and oppressed.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the qualification, cause-result, contrast, condition, information-focus and discourse patterns developed across all seventeen chapters.

exercises.title: Notice: How Sure Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Does the writer limit the claim, report others’ views, or say it for sure? Sort.
exercises.question: Which words show how far the writer stands behind each claim?

items: These caravans numbered up to 2,500 camels.
In a sense, they were serving as a media outlet.
The population of Mecca … was between 5,000 and 10,000.

dragDropGroups.group: The writer reports what others believed or said
items: Pre-Islamic Arabs thought the gods talked through kahins (soothsayers) and poets …
The leaders of the Quraysh viewed Islam as a threat to their authority.
The Quraysh were saying that Islam broke up families …

dragDropGroups.group: The writer states the claim with certainty
items: No doubt, pilgrimage to the Ka’ba was the most popular and common form of worship.
… it certainly doesn’t make sense to call the pre-Islamic era entirely negative.

The writer limits the claim: These caravans numbered up to 2,500 camels.
In a sense, they were serving as a media outlet.
The population of Mecca … was between 5,000 and 10,000.
The writer reports what others believed: Pre-Islamic Arabs thought the gods talked through kahins (soothsayers) and poets …
The leaders of the Quraysh viewed Islam as a threat to their authority.
The Quraysh were saying that Islam broke up families …
The writer states the claim with certain: No doubt, pilgrimage to the Ka’ba was the most popular and common form of worship.
… it certainly doesn’t make sense to call the pre-Islamic era entirely negative.

exercises.explanation: A careful reader tracks how far the writer stands behind each claim. “Up to” gives an upper limit, a range (between … and …) admits that the exact number is unknown, and “in a sense” marks a comparison as only partly true. Verbs such as thought, viewed … as and were saying report the beliefs or words of other people, not the writer’s own view. “No doubt” and “certainly” present a claim as sure. If you remove these signals when you retell a text, you change what the writer actually claims.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated limited claims, reported views and certain claims.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the signal in each sentence: A limit (up to, in a sense, between … and …), a reporting verb (thought, viewed, were saying) or a word of certainty (no doubt, certainly).

exercises.title: Notice: Who Stays in Focus?
exercises.instructions: Read the lines from Chapters 8 and 15. Then choose the best explanation.
exercises.question: Chapter 8: “In such a society, orphans were oppressed, the weak were looked down on, and the poor were shown no mercy.” Chapter 15: “The cries of children dying of hunger began to be heard.” Why does the writer not say who did these actions?
options: History does not record who treated these people so badly.
To keep the reader’s attention on the people who suffered, not on the people who caused the suffering.
In English, a passive verb cannot be followed by a “by” phrase.
To show that each of these things happened only once.
exercises.explanation: In these passives the people who suffered (orphans, the weak, the poor, the children) stay at the center of the sentence, and the doer is left out. The doers are not unknown: Chapter 8 names them in a separate sentence, “those who oppressed and treated people unfairly were generally wealthy and powerful individuals”. When the doer matters, the writer adds a “by” phrase: “an agreement was made by some Quraysh tribes”. So the choice between passive and active shows what the writer wants the reader to look at.

feedback.correct: Correct. The passive keeps the victims and what happened to them in focus.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what stands at the front of each sentence: The people who suffered, or the people who acted? Then look for the sentence in Chapter 8 that names the oppressors.

exercises.title: Notice: What Does “Would” Tell Us?
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapters 15 and 16. Is the statement true or false?
exercises.question: Chapter 15: “They knew that the Prophet’s call to monotheism … would eventually bring them face to face with people who carried out these practices.” Chapter 16: “Leaders who built their authority on idols would lose both their political and economic influence if they lost their idols.” Statement: In both sentences, “would” reports something that had already happened.
exercises.explanation: False. In Chapter 15, “would” is the past form of “will”: after “They knew that …”, it shows what the leaders expected to happen later, seen from their point in the past. In Chapter 16, “would” gives an imagined result, and the if-clause uses the past simple (if they lost) for a situation that had not happened. In both sentences “would” looks forward from the past; it does not report a finished event. That is why the leaders were afraid: They could see what might happen.

feedback.correct: Correct. Here “would” looks forward: An expected future and an imagined result.
feedback.incorrect: Did the leaders already face these people, or lose their idols, at that moment? Read “They knew that …” and “if they lost …” again.

exercises.title: Build: Reason, Result or Concession?
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapters 3, 4, 12 and 14 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word gives a result, a reason, or a contrast?
exercises.fillBlanksText: … the Zamzam water had not yet been discovered, [blank] there was no population living there. … [blank] the surroundings of the city were not suitable for agriculture, people tried to make a living through trade. … [blank] they mainly worshipped idols, they believed “Allah” to be the creator. … These people, who saw themselves as superior to others [blank] their wealth, ignored the Qur’an’s commands …
exercises.explanation: “So” introduces a result: The water had not been found, so nobody lived there. “Since” can introduce a reason that the reader easily accepts, and it is followed by a clause with a subject and a verb. “Because of” is followed by a noun phrase (their wealth). “Although” admits one fact and then adds a second fact that seems to clash with it; it takes a clause, so “Despite”, which needs a noun phrase, does not fit. “However” links two separate sentences and cannot introduce a clause like these.

feedback.correct: Well done. You matched each link to its meaning and to what follows it.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask two questions: Is it a result, a reason or a contrast? And is it followed by a clause or by a noun phrase?

exercises.title: Build: Fix the Claim, Fix the Form
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake: a claim that is too strong, or a wrong verb. Tap it, then fix it.
exercises.question: Can you keep each sentence careful and correct?

errorItems.sentence: All of the first Muslims were the poor and the slaves.
In addition, major trade festivals such as Ukaz … were also holding during the sacred months.
Otherwise, he would leave unprotected by his tribe …

exercises.explanation: The chapter says “Many of the first Muslims …”: “many” describes a large part of the group, while “all” would claim that there were no exceptions, which is more than the evidence shows (“much” is for uncountable nouns). Festivals do not hold anything; people hold them, so the passive is needed: were also held. In the same way, a member who stepped outside his tribe’s views did not leave anyone; he was the one who would lose protection, so after “would” we need be + past participle: would be left unprotected.

feedback.correct: Well done. You removed the overclaim and chose the passive where the subject receives the action.
feedback.incorrect: First ask whether the claim is stronger than the chapter allows. Then ask who does the action: The festivals and the tribal member, or other people?

exercises.title: Build: Same Meaning, New Structure
exercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapters 7, 8 and 14 by completing the frame. Keep the meaning of the original.
exercises.question: How else can we say these sentences from the book?

transformItems.source: Due to its fight against injustice, Hilf al-Fudul received support from the community.
transformItems.frame: Hilf al-Fudul received support from the community because [blank].

transformItems.source: Because large amounts of wealth were concentrated in the hands of certain individuals, there were extreme divisions between social classes.
transformItems.frame: Large amounts of wealth were concentrated in the hands of certain individuals. [blank], there were extreme divisions between social classes.

transformItems.source: The Quraysh were saying, “Muhammad is trying to gain the upper hand over us; …”
transformItems.frame: The Quraysh were saying that Muhammad [blank] to gain the upper hand over them.

exercises.explanation: “Due to” and “because of” are followed by a noun phrase (its fight against injustice); “because” is followed by a clause with its own subject and verb (it fought against injustice). A result can also open a new sentence with a linker such as As a result or Therefore. When direct speech is reported after a past verb (were saying that …), the present continuous moves back to the past continuous and the pronouns change: us → them. Reporting also reminds the reader that these are the Quraysh’s words, not the writer’s view.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the meaning and changed the structure correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Check what the frame needs: A clause after “because”, a result linker at the start of a sentence, and the past continuous with “them” after “were saying that”.

exercises.title: Build: Which Relative Word?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence from Chapters 8, 16 and 17.
exercises.question: Which word fits a person, and which fits a thing or a place?

formChoices.sentence: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), [choice] was twenty years old at the time, also attended this meeting.
The rejection of idols meant, for the Quraysh, the end of the trade on [choice] they depended for their wealth.
In Mecca, [choice] was a place of oppression, injustice, and immorality before Islam, the Prophet (pbuh) called upon people to follow justice and morality.

exercises.explanation: “Who” refers to a person, and in a clause between commas we cannot use “that”. After a preposition, “which” refers to a thing (on which they depended); “whom” is only for people, and “that” cannot follow a preposition. “Where” replaces an adverbial of place (the places where the disbelievers were sitting), but in Chapter 17 the relative word is the subject of “was”, so the writer needs “which”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the relative word by what it refers to and by its job in the clause.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what the word refers to (a person, a thing, a place) and what it does in its clause: Is it the subject, or does it follow a preposition?

exercises.title: Use: A Report on a School Project
exercises.instructions: This is part of a student report. Complete it with words from the bank. Two are not needed.
exercises.question: Can you report a school project carefully, without saying more than the evidence shows?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last term, a recycling project was started at our school by the student council. [blank] 40 bags of paper were collected every week, but the number changed from month to month. [blank] the project, the school needed to buy less new paper. [blank] some classes joined enthusiastically, others took part only occasionally. It can be said that the project was [blank] successful, but it is too early to call it a complete success. Next year, the council hopes that every class will take part.
exercises.explanation: Up to gives the highest weekly number, not the number for every week. As a result of + noun phrase names the cause of the saving. Although admits one fact and adds a contrasting one in the same sentence, without “but”; Despite would need a noun phrase. Mostly limits the success: The report praises the project but does not overclaim, which is why entirely does not fit. Like the writer of the book, a careful reporter keeps claims in proportion to the evidence.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your report is clear, fair and careful.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Is it a limit, a cause, a contrast or a degree? Then check what follows the gap: A number, a noun phrase or a clause.

exercises.title: Use: Say Only What the Evidence Shows
exercises.instructions: These sentences are new. Choose the words that say only what the facts show.
exercises.question: Which form keeps each new sentence accurate and fair?

formChoices.sentence: In our class survey, 18 of 25 students said they read every day, so [choice] students in our class read daily.
Each class may borrow [choice] 30 books a week: Some classes borrow 30, others borrow only 10 or 12.
Nobody saw who damaged the plants in the school garden, so the report says that the plants [choice] during the weekend.

exercises.explanation: Most matches 18 out of 25: a large part of the class, but not all of it. Up to gives the highest number allowed, so smaller numbers are still possible; exactly and at least do not fit a class that borrows only 10. When the doer is unknown, or less important than what happened, use the passive: The plants were damaged. The plants did not damage anything themselves.

feedback.correct: Well done. Each sentence now says exactly what the evidence shows.
feedback.incorrect: Compare each form with the evidence in the same sentence: How many, how much, and who did the action?

exercises.title: Use: Argue a Careful Case
exercises.instructions: Should your school have a student group that helps classmates treated unfairly? Write six to eight sentences.
exercises.question: What do you think, and why?
exercises.explanation: Example: “In my view, our school should set up a student committee to help classmates who are treated unfairly. At present, some students are left out or laughed at, and these problems are often not reported. Due to fear of being mocked, many students stay silent. As a result of this silence, small problems can grow into serious ones. Although our teachers already help, they cannot see everything that happens in the corridors. The committee would not replace the teachers; its role would be mostly to listen rather than to punish. If it worked fairly and respectfully, it would make our school a safer place for everyone.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: A clear position; a reason with because, due to or as a result of; a limit such as mostly, many, not always or although; a passive without “by” (students are left out …); and an if … would … sentence for a possible result.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Your view: “In my view, our school should … because …”
discussionPrompts.example: In my view, our school should set up a student committee because some classmates are treated unfairly and do not know where to go for help.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 2–3 — Reasons: “Some students are left out …”, “Due to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Some students are left out of group work or are not listened to in class. Due to fear of being laughed at, many of them stay silent, and as a result of this silence, small problems grow bigger.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 4–5 — Be careful: “Although …, …”, “… is not always …”
discussionPrompts.example: Although our teachers already help, they cannot see everything that happens during the breaks. The committee’s role would be mostly to listen rather than to punish because a complaint is not always a sign of a serious problem.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 6–7 — Results: “If the group …, it would … . Otherwise, …”
discussionPrompts.example: If the committee worked fairly and kept problems private, it would help every student feel safe at school. Otherwise, the unfair treatment would continue, and nobody would know about it.

pages.content: Demonstrate your deep mastership of the pre-Islamic Mecca historical and social systems at the B2 level.

exercises.title: A Qualified Judgment
exercises.instructions: Choose the reading that best matches the writer’s stance.
exercises.question: In Chapter 9 the writer says it “doesn’t make sense to call the pre-Islamic era entirely negative”. How does he then judge the Arabs’ famous generosity?
options: He presents it as proof that the era was mostly good.
He says it existed only in poems, not in real life.
He blames it on the Byzantine and Sassanid empires.
He admits it was real but says it came mostly from arrogance.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9 grants that “the Arabs before Islam were known for their extraordinary generosity and hospitality”, but adds: “The admirable qualities of the Arabs before Islam, like generosity, were driven mostly by arrogance rather than real goodness.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer gives credit and then limits it: The quality was real, but the motive was fame and pride.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 9. What does the writer say drove this generosity?

exercises.title: Not Always Wealthy
exercises.instructions: Choose the best interpretation.
exercises.question: Chapter 14 says the leading figures of the Quraysh “were not always extremely wealthy” and names Abu Talib. What does this detail add?
options: Leadership rested on standing within the tribe, not on wealth alone.
Abu Talib was the richest man among the first Muslims.
The poor were the true leaders of the Quraysh.
Wealth played no part in Meccan politics.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 14 says: “Indeed, almost none of the tribal leaders had accepted Islam. Although the leading figures of the Quraysh were not always extremely wealthy, they were prominent figures within the Quraysh, like Abu Talib.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer refines his picture: Wealth mattered, but a leader’s place in the tribe mattered too.
feedback.incorrect: Read the third paragraph of Chapter 14. What made these leaders important if not only wealth?

exercises.title: Hearing the Qur’an
exercises.instructions: Choose what the writer’s details emphasize.
exercises.question: Chapter 13 says the Qur’an made the first Muslims “cry and feel deep respect, even causing their hair to stand on end.” What do these details stress?
options: The Quraysh leaders forced the new Muslims to listen.
The message moved them in body and feeling, not only in thought.
The first Muslims did not yet understand the Qur’an.
The Prophet (pbuh) read the Qur’an only to his family.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “When they heard the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) read the Qur’an, they were sure it was from Allah. This message totally changed them. It touched their hearts and minds, making them cry and feel deep respect, even causing their hair to stand on end.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer moves from certainty in the mind to tears and physical reaction, to show how deep the change was.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 13. What happened to the listeners’ bodies and feelings?

exercises.title: Who Formed the Alliance?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is supported by the story.
exercises.question: Hilf al-Fudul was formed by the city’s wealthy oppressors to protect their own trade.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8 says: “an agreement was made by some Quraysh tribes to help people who had been oppressed in Mecca.” It also says: “those who oppressed and treated people unfairly were generally wealthy and powerful individuals.”

feedback.correct: Right. The alliance was made to protect the oppressed from the wealthy and powerful, not to serve them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 8. Whom was the agreement made to help?

exercises.title: The Pilgrimage Season

exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 11 with one word: justice, trade, poetry or travel.
exercises.question: What did extreme tribalism make impossible?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Tribes often formed a political alliance to defend each other, yet extreme tribalism made universal [blank] impossible when people supported their tribe even when it was wrong.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 ends: “Tribes often formed a political alliance to defend each other, yet extreme tribalism made universal justice impossible when people supported their tribe even when it was wrong.”

exercises.title: From the Valley to the Boycott
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: How does the history of Mecca unfold across the book?

sequencingItems.text: Young Muhammad joins Hilf al-Fudul at the age of twenty.
Abraham (pbuh) leaves Hagar and Ishmael in a valley without Zamzam.
The Meccan elites impose a boycott on the Muslims.
Hashim ibn Abd Manaf makes trade deals with other tribes and nations.
The Prophet’s call begins, and the Quraysh hear it first.

exercises.explanation: Hagar and Ishmael, about the 20th century BC (Chapter 3); Hashim, the Prophet’s great-grandfather (Chapter 5); Hilf al-Fudul, when the Prophet was twenty (Chapter 8); the call in 610 (Chapter 13); and the boycott between 617 and 620 (Chapter 15).

feedback.correct: Yes. The book moves from Mecca’s founding to its trade, then to the Prophet’s youth, his call and the pressure against it.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Hashim was the Prophet’s great-grandfather, so his trade deals came before the Prophet’s youth.
